cards.back: To formally put an end to a system, practice, or institution. Example: 'Several countries have abolished the death penalty in recent decades.'
A whole formed by combining several separate elements. Example: 'The aggregate of research findings supports the theory of climate change.'
Although; even though. Example: 'The experiment produced results, albeit not the ones the researchers had anticipated.'
The study of human societies, cultures, and their development. Example: 'Her coursework in anthropology examined kinship structures in indigenous communities.'
To absorb and integrate information, ideas, or culture. Example: 'Immigrants often assimilate the customs of their adopted country over time.'
The variety of plant and animal life in a particular habitat or ecosystem. Example: 'Tropical rainforests contain the greatest biodiversity of any terrestrial ecosystem.'
Something that causes an important event or change to happen more quickly. Example: 'The invention of the printing press was a catalyst for the spread of literacy in Europe.'
Arranged in the order of time in which events occurred. Example: 'The textbook presents historical events in chronological order from ancient to modern times.'
To quote or refer to a source as evidence or justification. Example: 'The professor asked students to cite at least ten peer-reviewed articles in their thesis.'
Evoking interest or attention in a powerfully convincing way. Example: 'The researcher presented compelling evidence that sleep deprivation impairs cognitive function.'
To consist of or be made up of certain parts. Example: 'The committee comprises twelve faculty members from different departments.'
A general agreement among a group of people. Example: 'The scientific consensus holds that human activity contributes significantly to global warming.'
To come together or assemble for a formal meeting or activity. Example: 'The academic senate convened to discuss changes to the university curriculum.'
A mutual relationship or connection between two or more things. Example: 'Researchers found a strong correlation between reading habits and academic performance.'
Relating to the statistical characteristics of a population. Example: 'Demographic shifts in the region have led to increased demand for multilingual education.'
To represent or show something in a picture, story, or description. Example: 'The mural depicts the migration of early settlers across the Great Plains.'
To officially assign a particular status or name to something. Example: 'The United Nations designated the area as a World Heritage Site in 1995.'
To make or become less in size, importance, or value. Example: 'Overfishing has significantly diminished the population of Atlantic bluefin tuna.'
To spread or distribute over a wide area. Example: 'Wind currents dispersed the volcanic ash across three continents.'
Recognizably different in nature from something else. Example: 'The study identified three distinct phases of language acquisition in young children.'
To tame an animal or cultivate a plant for human use. Example: 'Ancient peoples domesticated wheat approximately ten thousand years ago in the Fertile Crescent.'
To develop or present something in further detail. Example: 'The professor asked the student to elaborate on her hypothesis during the seminar.'
The production and discharge of something, especially gas or radiation. Example: 'Carbon emissions from industrial activity have increased steadily since the twentieth century.'
Based on observation or experience rather than theory or logic alone. Example: 'The researchers gathered empirical data through a series of controlled laboratory experiments.'
To surround or include a wide range of things. Example: 'The professor's lecture encompassed topics from evolutionary biology to modern genetics.'
The gradual wearing away of rock, soil, or land by natural forces. Example: 'Coastal erosion has threatened several archaeological sites along the Mediterranean.'
To apply or bring to bear a force, influence, or quality. Example: 'Ocean currents exert a powerful influence on regional climate patterns.'
No longer in existence, having died out completely. Example: 'The passenger pigeon became extinct in the early twentieth century due to overhunting.'
To make an action or process easier or more achievable. Example: 'The new software facilitates collaboration between researchers at different universities.'
To rise and fall irregularly in number or amount. Example: 'Global oil prices fluctuate in response to geopolitical events and supply changes.'
The preserved remains or traces of an organism from a past geological age. Example: 'Paleontologists discovered fossils that provided new insights into dinosaur behavior.'
The natural home or environment of an animal, plant, or organism. Example: 'Deforestation has destroyed the habitat of countless species in the Amazon basin.'

A proposed explanation made on the basis of limited evidence as a starting point for investigation. Example: 'The researcher's hypothesis was that increased sunlight exposure would accelerate plant growth.'
Originating or occurring naturally in a particular place; native. Example: 'The lecture focused on the indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest and their cultural traditions.'
The basic physical and organizational structures needed for a society to function. Example: 'Investing in transportation infrastructure is essential for economic development in rural regions.'
Existing as a natural or permanent quality of something. Example: 'There are inherent limitations in using self-reported surveys to measure behavioral changes.'
The supply of water to land or crops through artificial channels. Example: 'Ancient Mesopotamian civilizations developed sophisticated irrigation systems to support agriculture.'
Relating to language or the scientific study of language. Example: 'The researcher examined the linguistic diversity of communities along the Silk Road.'
The great size or importance of something. Example: 'Scientists measured the magnitude of the earthquake at 7.2 on the Richter scale.'
The chemical processes in a living organism that maintain life. Example: 'Cold-blooded animals have a slower metabolism than warm-blooded species.'
To move from one region or habitat to another, especially seasonally. Example: 'Millions of wildebeest migrate across the Serengeti each year in search of fresh grazing land.'
A fact or situation that is observed to exist or happen. Example: 'The Northern Lights are a natural phenomenon caused by solar particles entering the atmosphere.'
The process by which green plants use sunlight to convert carbon dioxide and water into food. Example: 'Photosynthesis is the foundation of nearly all food chains on Earth.'
Happening before a more important action or event; preparatory. Example: 'Preliminary findings suggest that the new drug may reduce symptoms by up to forty percent.'
Widespread or commonly occurring in a particular area or at a particular time. Example: 'Malaria remains prevalent in tropical regions where mosquito populations are high.'
The state of being near in space, time, or relationship. Example: 'The proximity of the university to the research hospital enabled close collaboration between faculty and clinicians.'
To make an exact copy of something or to reproduce a result. Example: 'Other laboratories attempted to replicate the experiment but obtained different results.'
Matter that settles to the bottom of a liquid or is deposited by water or wind. Example: 'Layers of sediment at the bottom of the lake revealed thousands of years of climate history.'
A thing or event that provokes a specific reaction or response. Example: 'The experiment measured how quickly subjects responded to a visual stimulus on the screen.'
The ability to maintain ecological balance without depleting natural resources. Example: 'The conference addressed sustainability challenges facing developing nations in the twenty-first century.'
